lessons.title: Introduction to Cloud Computing and AWS

content.title: Cloud Computing
content.text: Cloud computing provides computing resources such as servers, storage and databases over the internet instead of requiring users to maintain all infrastructure locally.

content.title: Amazon Web Services
content.text: AWS is a cloud platform that provides many services for computing, storage, databases, networking, security, analytics and application development.

content.title: Infrastructure as a Service
content.text: IaaS provides infrastructure resources such as virtual machines, storage and networking that users can configure and manage.

content.title: Platform as a Service
content.text: PaaS provides a managed platform for developing and deploying applications without requiring users to manage all underlying infrastructure.

content.title: Software as a Service
content.text: SaaS provides complete software applications through the internet.

key_points: Cloud computing provides resources over the internet.
AWS provides many cloud services.
IaaS provides infrastructure resources.
PaaS provides managed application platforms.
SaaS provides complete software applications.

lessons.title: AWS Global Infrastructure

content.title: AWS Regions
content.text: An AWS Region is a separate geographic area containing AWS infrastructure.

content.title: Availability Zones
content.text: Availability Zones are isolated locations within an AWS Region. Using multiple Availability Zones can improve application availability.

content.title: Choosing a Region
content.text: Region selection can depend on latency, service availability, regulatory requirements and cost.

content.title: Edge Locations
content.text: Edge locations support AWS services that deliver content and other resources closer to end users.

key_points: Regions represent geographic areas.
Availability Zones are isolated locations within Regions.
Multiple Availability Zones can improve availability.
Region selection affects latency and service availability.

lessons.title: Amazon EC2 and Cloud Computing

content.title: What is EC2?
content.text: Amazon EC2 provides resizable virtual computing capacity in the AWS cloud.

content.title: EC2 Instances
content.text: An EC2 instance is a virtual server running in AWS. Users can select instance configurations according to application requirements.

content.title: Amazon Machine Images
content.text: An AMI provides the information required to launch an EC2 instance, including the operating system and other configuration information.

content.title: Instance Types
content.text: Different EC2 instance families are designed for different workloads, including general purpose, compute optimized and memory optimized workloads.

content.title: Security Groups
content.text: Security groups act as virtual firewalls that control network traffic to and from EC2 instances.

key_points: EC2 provides virtual computing capacity.
Instances are virtual servers.
AMIs are used to launch instances.
Instance types are designed for different workloads.
Security groups control network traffic.

lessons.title: Amazon S3 and Cloud Storage

content.title: What is S3?
content.text: Amazon Simple Storage Service, or S3, is an object storage service designed to store and retrieve data.

content.title: Buckets
content.text: S3 stores objects inside containers called buckets. Bucket names must follow AWS naming requirements.

content.title: Objects
content.text: An S3 object consists of data and associated metadata. Objects are stored within buckets.

content.title: Storage Classes
content.text: S3 provides different storage classes designed for different access patterns and storage requirements.

content.title: Common Uses
content.text: S3 can be used for backups, datasets, application assets, static website files and other forms of object storage.

key_points: S3 is an object storage service.
Objects are stored in buckets.
S3 provides multiple storage classes.
S3 can store backups and application data.

lessons.title: AWS Databases

content.title: Amazon RDS
content.text: Amazon Relational Database Service helps users set up, operate and scale relational databases in AWS.

content.title: Relational Databases
content.text: Relational databases organize structured data into tables and use relationships between data entities.

content.title: DynamoDB
content.text: Amazon DynamoDB is a managed NoSQL database service designed for applications requiring scalable and low-latency data access.

content.title: RDS vs DynamoDB
content.text: RDS is designed for relational database workloads, while DynamoDB is a NoSQL database service.

key_points: RDS is a managed relational database service.
Relational databases organize data into tables.
DynamoDB is a managed NoSQL database.
Database choice depends on application requirements.

lessons.title: IAM and AWS Security

content.title: What is IAM?
content.text: AWS Identity and Access Management controls authentication and authorization for AWS resources.

content.title: IAM Users
content.text: IAM users represent identities that can be given permissions to access AWS resources.

content.title: IAM Roles
content.text: IAM roles provide permissions that can be assumed by trusted entities such as applications or AWS services.

content.title: Policies
content.text: IAM policies define permissions describing which actions are allowed or denied on specified resources.

content.title: Least Privilege
content.text: The principle of least privilege means providing only the permissions required to perform a task.

key_points: IAM manages access to AWS resources.
Users represent identities.
Roles provide permissions that can be assumed.
Policies define permissions.
Least privilege reduces unnecessary access.

lessons.title: AWS Lambda and Serverless Computing

content.title: What is AWS Lambda?
content.text: AWS Lambda is a serverless compute service that runs code in response to events without requiring users to manage servers.

content.title: Lambda Functions
content.text: A Lambda function contains the code executed when the function is invoked.

content.title: Event Driven Execution
content.text: Lambda functions can be invoked by events from AWS services or applications.

content.title: Serverless
content.text: Serverless computing allows developers to focus on application code while the cloud provider manages the underlying infrastructure.

content.title: Common Uses
content.text: Lambda can be used for APIs, data processing, automation, scheduled tasks and event-driven applications.

key_points: Lambda runs code without requiring server management.
Functions can be triggered by events.
Serverless reduces infrastructure management.
Lambda is useful for event-driven applications.
